topic.title: A 'no' in arranged marriage costs different people differently
topic.claim: In the arranged-marriage market, saying no is free for one side, and the other side can pay for it with her reputation.
topic.behaviour: A poster describes a friend who rejects matches by telling the girls' fathers made-up things, such as that the daughter has a boyfriend, and who is backed by the friend circle. The poster is shocked and wants out of the group.
topic.mechanism: Rejection happens between families through phone calls, without an appeal or a witness. When a past hurt meets that setup, a bitter person can turn it into a quiet weapon, and the group's silence tells him it's fine. The system relies on word of mouth and gives the woman's side little way to answer.
topic.group: young adults in the arranged-marriage market and their friend circles
real_details: A 28-year-old man is meeting girls through arranged marriage
He rejects them by saying fake things about the matches
He told one father that his daughter had a boyfriend and wasn't serious about AM
He has recently rejected two girls this way
The poster says the friend circle supported his decision
The poster doesn't want to stay in the friend group
topic.why_now: The wedding and matchmaking season is picking up, and the post got strong traction on the subreddit.

score.why: Pushes the matrimony-filter insight one notch further: saying no is free for one side and costs the other her name, the kind of asymmetry he likes to name.
